objective.statement: Optional extra practice: choose an approach chord before a cadence.
successCriteria: I know an approach chord comes just before the two cadence chords.
I can choose one from I, ii, IV or V that fits the melody note and differs from the first cadence chord.
I know this lesson is extra practice: the approach chord is taught in the cadence-choice lesson.

explanation.text: This lesson is extra practice. The approach chord is taught in the lesson on choosing chords at cadence points, and it can be asked in the Grade 5 assessment; here you can practise it further.

An approach chord is a chord before two cadence chords, so that three chords make a short progression: for example IV, ii, V or IV, V, I. At Grade 5 a suitable approach chord can always be found among I, ii, IV and V.
Choose the cadence chords first. Then pick any of I, ii, IV or V that contains the melody note before them.

music.textAlternative: Three chords in C major: IV, ii, V.

steps: The cadence is the last two chords: ii–V.
The chord before them is IV.
demonstration.textAlternative: IV, ii, V in C major.

guided.prompt: In G major, B and C make a perfect cadence. The chord at A comes BEFORE the cadence chords: it is an approach chord. Choose a chord for each of A, B and C (I, ii, IV or V), each containing its melody note, so that B and C make the cadence. (The approach chord may be any of I, ii, IV or V that fits the melody note.)

music.textAlternative: A treble-clef stave, key signature of 1 sharp, 4/4. Bar 1: a note on the 1st ledger line above the stave; a note on the 5th line; a note on the 4th line; a note marked A on the 3rd line. Bar 2: a note marked B on the 4th line; a note marked C in the space just above the stave.

hints: First choose the cadence chords for B and C. Then pick a chord for A that contains its melody note and is different from the chord at B: a cadence needs two different chords.

feedback.correct: Yes: the approach chord holds its melody note.

mistakes.chord-lacks-melody-note: Each chord must contain its melody note.
mistakes.non-cadential-pair: Cadences are V–I, IV–I, or end on V.
mistakes.cadence-misnamed: Name the last two chords first: V–I perfect, IV–I plagal, ending on V imperfect.
mistakes.wrong-key: Check the key signature and the final note — then build the chords in that key.

feedback.fallback: Not quite. For each marked note, list the chords that contain it, then choose a pair that makes a cadence.

mastery.completion: Optional extra practice with approach chords. It is complete when every step has been answered correctly. It is never required and gates no other node; its answers count as practice of choosing chords at cadence points, like any other practice of that concept.

provenance.authoredBy: Music Theory Path curriculum team (Brief 05, drafted with AI assistance; pending qualified teacher review)
provenance.notes: Extra practice only (the approach chord itself is compulsory since the review of PR #13: First Steps Grade 5 section 11, pp. 124-126, and every practice paper sets five chord boxes split 2 + 3). The grader accepts any chord of I, ii, IV or V that holds the melody note and is not the chord at B.
